H1.text: A ceiling fan has three flat blades. A seesaw is one straight line. A sea wall block has four legs, and one always points up.

H2.text: Three shapes. Carbon can make every one of them.

H3.text: Diya sees it in the kitchen. She pushes four toothpicks into a small ball of dough.

H4.text: She spreads them as far apart as she can. However it lands, one toothpick points straight up.

H5.text: Carbon does the same with its bonds. By the end, you will know its shape just by counting bonds.

P1.text: Welcome to a new chapter. Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds.

P2.text: Sugar, cotton, cooking gas, even you. All built on carbon.

P3.text: People once thought only living things could make these. In eighteen twenty eight, Wohler made urea in a lab, from a salt.

P4.text: So what is so special about carbon? Its electrons are arranged two, then four. Four electrons in the outer shell.

P5.text: Each outer electron can pair with one from another atom. So carbon makes four bonds, like four hands.

P6.text: Having four bonds is called being tetravalent. Tetra means four.

S1.text: Let's see how carbon shapes those four hands, on our molecule bench.

S2.text: Carbon starts with two electrons in 2s and two in 2p. Only two are unpaired.

S3.text: One 2s electron jumps up to the empty 2p. This is promotion. Now four are unpaired.

S4.text: Then the orbitals blend. One s and three p make four equal s p three orbitals.

S5.text: They push as far apart as they can, to the corners of a tetrahedron, at one hundred and nine point five degrees. Four single bonds, like in methane.

B1.text: When carbon makes a double bond, it mixes one s with only two p. Three s p two orbitals, flat, at one hundred and twenty degrees, like in ethene.

B2.text: One p orbital is left over. It stands straight up, ready for the double bond.

B3.text: With a triple bond, it mixes one s with one p. Two s p orbitals, in a straight line, at one hundred and eighty degrees, like in ethyne. Two p are left over.

B4.text: So the s share goes up. Twenty five percent in s p three, about thirty three in s p two, and fifty in s p. This share is called s character.

D1.text: Why does s character matter? Link by link.

D2.text: Link one. An s orbital sits closer to the nucleus than a p orbital.

D3.text: Link two. So the more s character, the closer the bonding electrons stay to the carbon.

D4.text: Link three. So bonds get shorter. Carbon to carbon is one hundred fifty four picometres in ethane, one hundred thirty four in ethene, one hundred twenty in ethyne.

D5.text: Link four. Shorter bonds are stronger. The double bond needs six hundred eighty one kilojoules per mole to break. The single bond, only three hundred forty eight.

D6.text: Link five. Electrons held close also make the carbon pull harder. So an s p carbon is the most electronegative.

C1.text: Now look closely at the double bond itself. Ethane and ethene, side by side.

C2.text: In ethane, the two carbons share one sigma bond, end to end. Each end can spin, like a wheel on its axle.

C3.text: In ethene, the leftover p orbitals stand side by side and overlap sideways. That extra bond is a pi bond. All six atoms lie flat in one plane.

C4.text: Pause and think. Can the two ends of ethene spin, like the ends of ethane?

C5.text: No! A twist turns the p orbitals away from each other, and the pi bond breaks. So rotation about a double bond is restricted.

C6.text: The pi cloud sits above and below the plane, out in the open. Attackers reach it easily. So pi bonds are the most reactive spots.

T1.text: Remember this. Count carbon's bonds, and you know its shape.

W1.text: Now, one worked example. Find each carbon's hybridisation, and count the sigma and pi bonds.

W2.text: Step one. Carbons one and two share a double bond. Each makes three sigma bonds, so both are s p two.

W3.text: Step two. Carbons three and four share a triple bond. Each makes two sigma bonds, so both are s p.

W4.text: Step three. Count sigma bonds. Every bond has exactly one. Three carbon to carbon, four carbon to hydrogen. Seven sigma.

W5.text: Step four. Count pi bonds. One in the double bond, two in the triple bond. Three pi.

W6.text: So the left end is flat, and the right end is a straight line.

X2.text: Students say a double bond is just two single bonds, so it must be twice as strong.

X3.text: Wrong. It is one sigma plus one weaker pi. Three hundred ninety seven plus two hundred eighty four is six hundred eighty one. Less than twice three hundred forty eight.

E1.text: Where is this asked? Boards and entrance tests ask for each carbon's hybridisation, sigma and pi counts, and bond lengths.

Q1.text: Exam level now. What is the hybridisation of each carbon, left to right, in this molecule? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. s p two, s p two, s p three, s p.

A2.text: The first two carbons share a double bond, so both are s p two.

A3.text: The middle C H two has four single bonds, so it is s p three.

A4.text: The last carbon has a triple bond to nitrogen, so it is s p. B traps students who count four bonds and say s p three.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why is carbon called tetravalent?

Y3.text: Two. Which is shorter, the carbon bond in ethene or in ethyne?

Y4.text: Three. Why can't the two ends of a double bond spin?
